column6: Central to the birth of Gnosticism; the birthplace of Valentinus and home of Basilides.
Marcion preached here around 150 and Valentinus stood as a candidate for bishop.
Twelve codices, perhaps buried after Athanasius's Festal Letter of 367, were found near here in 1945.
Jules Doinel re-established a Gnostic church in France in 1890.

column3: By the mid-2nd century Gnostic systems are fully developed in the Mediterranean, with Alexandria central to their birth; Marcion preaches in Rome around 150.
Valentinianism, an intellectually vibrant school, spreads to Northwest Africa, Egypt, Asia Minor and Syria, and Irenaeus writes against the Gnostics (c. 180–185).
Sethianism is a main current of Gnosticism, and Plotinus and later Neoplatonists attack it; decline sets in during the 3rd century.
Athanasius condemns non-canonical books in 367; the Nag Hammadi codices may have been buried soon after.
Gnostic groups fade in the Mediterranean as orthodoxy settles; Basilidians in Egypt survive to the end of the 4th century and Gnosticism persists in the Near East until at least the 6th century.
On the edge of the Byzantine world the Paulicians arise, accused by medieval sources of being Gnostic, and the Mandaeans continue in southern Mesopotamia.
The Bogomils emerge in Bulgaria between 927 and 970; the Cathars are later accused of Gnostic traits, though a direct link is disputed.
The Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) and conversion to Islam greatly reduce the remaining Gnostics.
Jules Doinel re-establishes a Gnostic church in France in 1890.
The discovery of the Nag Hammadi library renews interest, and modern Gnostic churches are founded; the Mandaeans, 60,000 to 70,000 worldwide, live in Iraq, Iran and diaspora communities.
